lessons.title: Place value and large numbers
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB National Syllabus, Mathematics, Level III (Classes 5-6) — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Read, write and compare numbers up to hundreds of millions.
Give the value of a digit in a large number.
Round a number to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000 or 100,000.
reviewNotes: Names of places above millions (billions) are left out; the Class 6 syllabus limit (millions or hundreds of millions) is to be checked.
Use of commas vs spaces to group digits: commas used here, as in Cameroonian anglophone textbooks (to be checked).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Place value
blocks.md: The **value** of a digit depends on its **place** in the number. In 4,236,508 the digit 2 is in the hundred-thousands place, so its value is 200,000. The digit 3 is in the ten-thousands place, so its value is 30,000.

items.text: M = millions   HTh = hundred thousands   TTh = ten thousands
Th = thousands   H = hundreds   T = tens   O = ones

blocks.caption: The number 4,236,508 in a place-value table.
blocks.alt: A table with seven boxes. The headings are M, HTh, TTh, Th, H, T and O. Under them are the digits 4, 2, 3, 6, 5, 0 and 8.

blocks.title: Reading big numbers
blocks.md: Group the digits in threes from the right: 4,236,508. Read each group and add its name. We say: four **million**, two hundred and thirty-six **thousand**, five hundred and eight. A zero in a place means that place is empty, but we must write the zero.

blocks.title: Rounding
blocks.md: To round to the nearest 1,000: look at the digit just on the right (the hundreds digit). If it is **5 or more**, add one to the thousands digit. If it is **less than 5**, keep it. Then put zeros after. Example: 365,482 gives 365,000 because the hundreds digit is 4.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Writing 'four million two hundred thirty-six' for 4,236,508: you forget the thousands.
- Confusing the **digit** (3) with its **value** (30,000).
- Dropping a zero: five million and sixty-three is 5,000,063, not 563.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Write 4,236,508 in words. What is the value of the digit 3?
steps: Read: four million, two hundred and thirty-six thousand, five hundred and eight.
The 3 is in the ten-thousands place: its value is 3 × 10,000 = 30,000.
blocks.answer: Four million, two hundred and thirty-six thousand, five hundred and eight; the value of 3 is 30,000.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Round 365,482 to the nearest 1,000 and to the nearest 10,000.
steps: Nearest 1,000: the hundreds digit is 4 (less than 5), so we keep 365 thousand: 365,000.
Nearest 10,000: look at the thousands digit, 5. It is 5 or more, so the 6 ten-thousands becomes 7: 370,000.

objectives: Find the factors and multiples of a number.
Recognise prime numbers and write a number as a product of primes.
Find the HCF and the LCM of two or three numbers.
reviewNotes: Prime factorisation and HCF/LCM by prime factors are shown briefly; check that the syllabus expects the listing method.
Divisibility tests (by 3, 9...) are not covered in this lesson.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Factors and multiples
blocks.md: A **factor** of a number divides it exactly. The factors of 24 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12 and 24. A **multiple** of a number is in its times table: the multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24, 30... A **prime number** has exactly two factors, 1 and itself: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13... The number 1 is not prime.

blocks.caption: A factor tree for 60: 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5.
blocks.alt: A tree. 60 splits into 6 and 10. Then 6 splits into 2 and 3, and 10 splits into 2 and 5. The bottom numbers 2, 3, 2 and 5 are prime.

blocks.title: HCF and LCM
blocks.md: The **HCF** (highest common factor) is the biggest number that divides both numbers. The **LCM** (lowest common multiple) is the smallest number that both numbers divide. Method: list the factors (or multiples) of each number, then pick the biggest common factor (or the smallest common multiple).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Mixing up HCF and LCM: the HCF is **small** (never bigger than the numbers), the LCM is **big** (never smaller than the numbers).
- Saying that 1 is a prime number, or that 9 is prime (9 = 3 × 3).
- Forgetting that 2 is the only **even** prime number.

blocks.title: Example 1
steps: The common factors are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. The biggest is 12.

blocks.title: Example 2
steps: The first number in both lists is 36.

blocks.title: Number patterns
blocks.md: A **sequence** is a list of numbers that follows a rule. Each number is a **term**. In 3, 7, 11, 15... we **add 4** each time. In 2, 6, 18, 54... we **multiply by 3** each time. To find the rule, look at the difference or the ratio between neighbouring terms.

blocks.caption: The first five square numbers: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25.
blocks.alt: A bar chart with five bars of growing height. The bars are 1, 4, 9, 16 and 25. They are the squares of 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5.

blocks.title: Rule for any term
blocks.md: For a pattern that adds the same number d each time and starts at a, the term number n is: a + (n − 1) × d. Example: 3, 7, 11, 15... has a = 3 and d = 4. The 20th term is 3 + 19 × 4 = 79.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Checking only the first two terms. Always check the rule on **all** the terms you know.
- In the 'n-th term' formula, using n × d instead of (n − 1) × d: the first term has no jump yet.

blocks.title: Example 2
steps: The first term is 4 and we add 3 each time.

exercises.prompt: What is the value of the digit 7 in 3,472,150?
exercises.explanation: The 7 is in the ten-thousands place: 7 × 10,000 = 70,000.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Which number is the largest?
exercises.explanation: Compare the millions first (all 1), then the hundred-thousands digit: 9 is the biggest in 1,905,000.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Round 8,649,731 to the nearest 100,000.
exercises.explanation: The ten-thousands digit is 4 (less than 5), so we keep 8,600,000.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: In 5,060,203 the digit 6 has the value 60,000.
exercises.explanation: 5,060,203: the 5 is millions, the 0 hundred-thousands, the 6 ten-thousands. So 6 is worth 60,000.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Write as a number: 2 millions, 5 ten-thousands, 7 hundreds and 3 ones.
exercises.explanation: 2,000,000 + 50,000 + 700 + 3 = 2,050,703. The empty places (hundred-thousands, thousands, tens) are zeros.

parts.explanation: The 4 is in the hundred-thousands place: 400,000.

parts.prompt: Round the mass to the nearest 100,000 kg.
parts.explanation: The ten-thousands digit is 7, so we round up: 3,500,000.

parts.prompt: How many more kilograms are needed to reach 4,000,000 kg?

exercises.prompt: What is the value of 5 in 6,250,310?
exercises.explanation: The 5 is in the ten-thousands place.

exercises.prompt: How do we write 'two million, forty thousand and nine'?
exercises.explanation: 2,000,000 + 40,000 + 9. Empty places are zeros.

exercises.prompt: Round 74,860 to the nearest 1,000.
exercises.explanation: The hundreds digit is 8, so round up to 75,000.

exercises.prompt: Which is smaller: 3,099,999 or 3,100,000?
exercises.explanation: Both have 3 millions; 099,999 is less than 100,000.

exercises.prompt: In 9,008,004 how many hundred-thousands are there?
exercises.explanation: The hundred-thousands place holds 0.

exercises.prompt: Which of these numbers is prime?
exercises.explanation: 21 = 3 × 7, 27 = 3 × 9 and 39 = 3 × 13. Only 29 has just two factors.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Find the HCF of 18 and 45.
exercises.explanation: Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. Factors of 45: 1, 3, 5, 9, 15, 45. The biggest common one is 9.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Find the LCM of 15 and 20.
exercises.explanation: Multiples of 20: 20, 40, 60. 60 is also a multiple of 15 (15 × 4).

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: How many factors does 24 have?

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Find the LCM of 4, 6 and 10.
exercises.explanation: Multiples of 10: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60. The first one that 4 and 6 also divide is 60.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: A baker in Bafoussam packs 48 buns and 72 puff-puffs into identical bags. Each bag has the same number of buns and the same number of puff-puffs, with nothing left over. He wants as many bags as possible.

parts.prompt: How many bags can he make?
How many buns are in each bag?
How many puff-puffs are in each bag?

exercises.prompt: Which number is a factor of 30?
exercises.explanation: 30 ÷ 15 = 2 exactly. The others do not divide 30.

exercises.prompt: What is the HCF of 12 and 30?
exercises.explanation: Common factors are 1, 2, 3, 6. The highest is 6.

exercises.prompt: What is the LCM of 6 and 8?
exercises.explanation: Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24. 24 is a multiple of 6 too.

exercises.prompt: Which list has only prime numbers?
exercises.explanation: 9 and 15 are not prime and 1 is not prime.

exercises.prompt: Two bells ring every 4 minutes and every 6 minutes. They ring together now. After how many minutes will they ring together again?
exercises.explanation: LCM of 4 and 6 is 12.

exercises.explanation: These are square numbers: 5 × 5 = 25.

exercises.prompt: What is the rule of 80, 40, 20, 10?
exercises.explanation: Each term is half of the one before.

exercises.prompt: Which sequence is made of even numbers only?

exercises.explanation: It is the 3 times table: 3 × 10 = 30.
